<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:korselt}
$n$ is a Carmichael number if and only if $n$ is composite, square-free, and $(p-1) \mid (n-1)$ for every prime $p \mid n$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
The count $C(B)$ of Carmichael numbers less than $B$ satisfies
\[ C(B) \leq B \exp \left\{ \frac{-(1 - o(1))\log B \log \log \log B}{ \log \log B }\right\}.\]
We let $\mathcal{E}(B)$ denote this bound.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:dmin}
Let $n$ be a CN and $d \mid n$ a divisor with $d \cdot \lambda(d) > n$. Then $k = 0$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $d$ be a divisor of a CN $n$ with $d \cdot\lambda(d) > n$.
Then $n = d\cdot r^\star$.
If $k > 0$, then $n = d(r^\star + k\lambda(d)) > d \cdot\lambda(d) > n $, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:alpha}
Every child $vq$ of a node $v$ satisfies $q \nmid \lambda_v$ and $\gcd(q - 1, d_v) = 1$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Choose $n \in \mathcal{C}_B$ whose path passes through $vq$.
Each prime $p$ of $d_v$ divides $n$, so $(p - 1) \mid (n - 1)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:korselt}, and therefore $\lambda_v \mid n - 1$.
Since $q \mid n$, $q \nmid (n - 1)$, so $q \nmid \lambda_v$.
Symmetrically, $(q - 1) \mid (n - 1)$ and $d_v \mid n$, so $\gcd(q - 1, d_v)$ divides $\gcd(n - 1, n) = 1$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:decode}
For every $n \in \mathcal{C}_B$, the terminal node $v = v_{\pi(n)}$ determines $n = d_v \cdot r_v^\star$, where $r_v^\star = d_v^{-1} \bmod \lambda_v$.
Hence $n \mapsto v_{\pi(n)}$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{C}_B$ onto the terminal nodes of $T$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The divisor $d_v$ stored for $n$ is stopping, so Proposition~\ref{prop:dmin} gives $n = d_v \cdot r_v^\star$.
The map is onto the terminal nodes by their definition, and it is one-to-one because $v_{\pi(n)} = v_{\pi(m)}$ gives $n = d_v r_v^\star = m$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:pwt}
$\mathrm{PWT}(T)$ with $t$ nodes decodes to $\mathcal{C}_B$ in polynomial time per node.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
One pre-order pass, visits children in sibling order and unranks each node's prime $q$.
We can then write $d_{vq} = d_v q$ via standard multiplication. 
The Euclidean algorithm computes $\lambda_{vq} = \mathrm{lcm}(\lambda_v, q - 1)$ and $r^\star \equiv d_v^{-1} \bmod{\lambda_v}$.  
Another multiplication computes $n = d_v \cdot r^\star$.
If the prime factors of $r^\star$ are needed, these can also obtained in polynomial time by Algorithm 1 of \cite{shallue-webster2026}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
